title: Panic Attack After Drinking: Why It Happens and What to Do
excerpt: Why alcohol can trigger panic attacks the night or morning after, how hangover panic differs from hangxiety, what to do in the moment, and when it needs a doctor.
metaDescription: Why hangover panic attacks happen, how they differ from hangxiety, how to calm one in the moment, and the signs that mean you should see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a panic attack after drinking is a real and surprisingly common experience, and in most people it's the brain's rebound from alcohol rather than a sign that something is seriously wrong. While you drink, alcohol pushes your brain toward calm. As it wears off, often in the middle of the night or the next morning, the brain overshoots in the other direction. Combine that with stress hormones, broken sleep, low blood sugar, dehydration, and a racing pulse, and your body can produce every physical sensation of a panic attack. The good news is that these attacks pass, there are simple things that help in the moment, and you can lower the odds of another one. The part to take seriously: a few symptoms overlap with heart problems and alcohol withdrawal, and those need a doctor, not a breathing exercise.

**The quick rules:** If it's happening right now, sit down, breathe out slowly (longer out than in), and remind yourself that panic peaks within minutes and then fades. Sip water, eat something small, and skip more caffeine. Don't drink more alcohol to calm down. Call 911 for chest pain or pressure, fainting, an irregular heartbeat, confusion, or symptoms that don't ease. If these attacks keep happening, or you need a drink in the morning to stop shaking, talk to a doctor.

> **When to see a doctor or call 911:** Call 911 (or your local emergency number) if you have **chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to your arm, jaw, neck, or back, fainting or nearly fainting, severe shortness of breath, a pulse that feels irregular or stays very fast at rest, confusion, seizures, or seeing or hearing things that aren't there**. Don't assume it's "just panic" if it's your first time, you're over about 40, or you have a heart condition, high blood pressure, or diabetes. Get checked by a doctor soon if panic attacks **keep happening after drinking**, happen **even when you haven't been drinking**, or you've started **avoiding places or situations** because of them. If you drink heavily most days and feel shaky, sweaty, panicky, or sick as alcohol wears off, that can be **alcohol withdrawal**, which can be dangerous. Don't drink more to make it stop, and don't ride it out alone. Get medical help. If you're having thoughts of harming yourself, call or text **988** (US) or your local crisis line. **This article is general information, not medical advice.**

## Hangover Panic Attacks vs Hangxiety: What's the Difference?

People use "hangxiety" for almost any anxious feeling after drinking, but a panic attack is a specific thing, and the difference matters for what you do about it.

**Hangxiety** is a slow, background feeling. You wake up with a sense of dread, replay what you said last night, feel restless and on edge, and can't quite settle. It can hang around for most of the day. We cover it in depth in our [complete guide to hangxiety](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research).

**A panic attack** is a sudden surge of intense fear or discomfort that builds quickly and peaks within minutes. The standard psychiatric definition (from the DSM-5, the manual doctors use to diagnose mental health conditions) describes it as an abrupt surge that comes with at least four of these symptoms:

- Pounding or racing heart
- Sweating
- Trembling or shaking
- Shortness of breath or a feeling of being smothered
- A choking feeling
- Chest pain or discomfort
- Nausea or stomach upset
- Feeling dizzy, unsteady, lightheaded, or faint
- Chills or hot flushes
- Numbness or tingling, often in the hands or around the mouth
- Feeling unreal or detached from yourself
- Fear of losing control or "going crazy"
- Fear of dying

Look at that list next to a bad hangover: racing heart, shakes, sweating, nausea, dizziness. A hangover already supplies half the symptoms of a panic attack before you've had a single anxious thought. That's a big part of why panic is more likely the morning after.

| | Hangxiety | Hangover panic attack |
|---|---|---|
| How it starts | Gradually, often on waking | Suddenly, sometimes out of nowhere |
| How long it lasts | Hours, sometimes all day | Peaks within about 10 minutes, mostly eases within 30 to 60 minutes |
| What it feels like | Worry, dread, guilt, restlessness | Intense fear plus strong body symptoms |
| Typical thought | "What did I say last night?" | "Something is very wrong with me right now" |
| Main fix | Rest, food, time, perspective | Ride out the wave, slow breathing, rule out anything medical |

The two overlap. A morning of hangxiety can tip into a panic attack, and after a panic attack you'll often feel a lingering hangxiety-style unease for the rest of the day.

## Why Alcohol Can Trigger a Panic Attack

There isn't one cause. Several things stack up at once, which is why one night of drinking can leave you fine and the next leaves you shaking on the bathroom floor at 4 a.m.

### 1. The brain's rebound effect

Your brain runs on a balance between calming and exciting signals. The main calming chemical messenger is **GABA**. The main exciting one is **glutamate**. Alcohol boosts GABA's effect and blocks some of glutamate's, which is why a couple of drinks make you feel relaxed and less inhibited.

Your brain doesn't like being pushed off balance, so while you drink it starts adjusting: it turns down its own calming system and turns up its excitatory one. When the alcohol leaves your system, those adjustments are still in place. For a few hours you're left with less brake and more accelerator than usual. Researchers often describe hangover anxiety as a mini version of withdrawal for exactly this reason. In someone who drinks occasionally, the effect is short-lived. In someone who drinks heavily every day, the same rebound can become full alcohol withdrawal, which is a medical issue (more on that below).

### 2. Stress hormones

Drinking raises cortisol, the body's main stress hormone, and a hangover is associated with a stress response in general. As alcohol wears off, your nervous system's "fight or flight" side is more active. Adrenaline speeds your heart, tightens your muscles, and sharpens your attention toward threats. That's the exact state in which a panic attack is easiest to set off.

### 3. Your heart is already racing

Alcohol widens your blood vessels and dehydrates you, and your heart speeds up to compensate. Many people wake after drinking with a pulse that's noticeably faster than normal. Panic often starts with noticing a body sensation, such as a thudding heart, and interpreting it as dangerous: "Why is my heart doing that? Is something wrong?" That fear releases more adrenaline, which makes the heart beat faster, which feels more alarming. This loop is the engine of most panic attacks. Our guide to a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains the heart side in detail, including when it's not just anxiety.

### 4. Broken sleep

Alcohol can help you fall asleep, but it disrupts the second half of the night. Many people wake around 3 or 4 a.m. feeling wired, sweaty, and alert, sometimes with a pounding heart. This is a common time for a panic attack: you're groggy, it's dark, there's nothing to distract you, and your brain is mid-rebound. Lack of sleep also lowers your tolerance for stress the next day. If waking in the night is your pattern, see our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking).

### 5. Low blood sugar

Alcohol interferes with your liver's ability to release stored sugar into your blood, especially if you drank without eating much. Low blood sugar causes shakiness, sweating, a fast heartbeat, irritability, and a sense of unease. These overlap so heavily with panic that your brain can easily mistake one for the other.

### 6. Dehydration

Alcohol makes you pass more urine than you take in. Mild dehydration can make you dizzy or lightheaded, especially when you stand up, and can make your heart work harder. Dizziness is one of the more frightening panic symptoms because it feels like you might faint or lose control.

### 7. Caffeine, nicotine, and other substances

The morning-after coffee is a common panic trigger. Caffeine is a stimulant that raises heart rate and adrenaline, and a hangover makes you more sensitive to it. Nicotine has a similar effect. Recreational drugs used on the same night, especially stimulants, raise the odds of a panic attack further. Some energy drink and alcohol combinations pack a lot of caffeine on top of the drinking itself.

### 8. Your mind replaying the night

Social worry plays a part too. Research from UK university teams has found that people who are more shy or socially anxious tend to report more anxiety during a hangover. If you already run anxious, a fuzzy memory of the night before gives your mind plenty of material to worry about, which lowers the threshold for panic.

## Panic During Drinking vs Panic the Next Morning

Panic attacks can show up at different points, and the likely cause differs a little.

**While drinking or soon after:** This is less common, because alcohol is still doing its calming work. When it happens, think about other triggers: a crowded or overwhelming setting, mixing alcohol with stimulants or cannabis, an energy drink cocktail, drinking fast on an empty stomach, or a flushing reaction. Some people (especially many people of East Asian descent) have a genetic variant that makes them build up a by-product of alcohol called acetaldehyde, which causes flushing, a fast heartbeat, and a pounding head that can feel a lot like panic.

**In the middle of the night:** This is the classic one. You wake suddenly at 3 or 4 a.m., heart pounding, sweating, sure something is wrong. This is usually the rebound effect meeting broken sleep.

**The next morning or afternoon:** This is the hangover panic attack. Your body is depleted, you're dehydrated, maybe a bit hypoglycemic, and maybe on your second coffee. A small trigger, like a stressful message or a sudden head rush when you stand up, sets it off.

**A day or more later in someone who drinks heavily:** If you drink a lot most days and panic, shaking, sweating, or nausea start 6 to 24 hours after your last drink, this isn't a normal hangover. It can be alcohol withdrawal. See the warning section below.

## What to Do During a Panic Attack After Drinking

A panic attack feels like an emergency, but the panic itself can't hurt you. It's your body's alarm system firing at the wrong time. The goal isn't to force it to stop, which tends to make it worse. It's to let the wave rise and fall without adding fuel. If anything on the "call 911" list is happening, deal with that first.

### Step 1: Name it

Say to yourself, out loud if it helps: "This is a panic attack. My body is reacting to alcohol wearing off. It will peak and pass." Naming it shifts you out of the "something is terribly wrong" story that keeps the loop going.

### Step 2: Slow your breathing, especially the out-breath

Panic often comes with fast, shallow breathing, which lowers carbon dioxide in your blood and causes tingling, dizziness, and a tight chest. Slow it down:

- Breathe in gently through your nose for about 4 seconds.
- Breathe out slowly through pursed lips for about 6 to 8 seconds.
- Keep going for a few minutes.

The long exhale engages the "rest and digest" side of your nervous system, which gently slows your heart. Don't take huge gulps of air. Small, slow, and steady is the aim. Breathing into a paper bag is no longer recommended.

### Step 3: Ground yourself

Pull your attention outward instead of inward. A common technique is 5-4-3-2-1: name five things you can see, four you can touch, three you can hear, two you can smell, and one you can taste. Pressing your feet into the floor or holding something cold also helps. Splashing cold water on your face can calm a racing heart for some people.

### Step 4: Let it pass without fighting

Panic peaks within minutes. Rather than checking your pulse over and over or searching your symptoms, let the sensations be there. People often find the attack fades faster when they stop trying to push it away.

### Step 5: Look after your body once it eases

- **Drink water.** Sip steadily. If you've been sick, an electrolyte drink is a good option. See our guide on [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking).
- **Eat something simple.** Toast, a banana, crackers, or oatmeal help steady your blood sugar.
- **Skip caffeine for a few hours.** If you're used to coffee and worried about a withdrawal headache, have a small cup later, once you're steady.
- **Rest.** A short nap or just lying down in a quiet room gives your nervous system a chance to settle.
- **Move gently.** A slow walk outside can burn off some of the adrenaline.

### What not to do

- **Don't drink more alcohol.** "Hair of the dog" may blunt the feeling for a short time, but it delays the rebound rather than ending it and teaches your brain to reach for alcohol to feel calm.
- **Don't take sedatives or someone else's anxiety medicine.** Benzodiazepines like Xanax combined with alcohol still in your system can dangerously slow your breathing. Our page on [Xanax and alcohol](/never-hungover/xanax-and-alcohol) explains why.
- **Don't pile on stimulants.** More coffee, energy drinks, or nicotine will usually make things worse.

## Is It Panic, a Heart Problem, or Withdrawal?

This is the most important section on this page. Panic is the most common explanation for these symptoms after a night of drinking, but it isn't the only one, and you can't always tell from the inside.

### Signs it's more likely panic

- It came on fast and peaked within about 10 minutes.
- It eases with slow breathing, distraction, or time.
- You've had similar episodes before that were checked and turned out to be panic.
- Your pulse is fast but steady and regular.

### Signs to treat it as a possible heart problem

- **Crushing, squeezing, or heavy chest pain**, especially if it spreads to the arm, jaw, neck, or back.
- **Fainting or nearly fainting.**
- **An irregular pulse**, skipping, chaotic, or uneven rather than just fast.
- Symptoms that **don't settle** after 20 to 30 minutes or keep coming back in waves for hours.
- You're **older**, have heart disease, high blood pressure, diabetes, or a family history of early heart problems.

Alcohol, especially a big night, can trigger an irregular heart rhythm called atrial fibrillation (AFib). It's sometimes called "holiday heart" because it shows up after holiday binges. It needs medical attention. If you're not sure, call 911 or go to an emergency room. Being checked and told it was panic is a good outcome, not a wasted trip.

### Signs it may be alcohol withdrawal

Withdrawal isn't just a problem for people who think of themselves as having a drinking problem. It can happen to anyone whose body has adapted to regular heavy drinking. Signs include:

- Shaking or tremor, especially in the hands, that gets better when you drink
- Sweating, nausea, or vomiting starting 6 to 24 hours after your last drink
- Anxiety or panic that comes back every time you stop
- A racing heart and high blood pressure
- Trouble sleeping, vivid dreams, or feeling agitated
- In more serious cases, seeing or hearing things, confusion, or seizures

**Alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous**, and it's one of the few withdrawal syndromes that can be life-threatening. If these signs fit you, speak to a doctor rather than trying to cut down suddenly on your own. Severe symptoms such as confusion, hallucinations, seizures, or a high fever are an emergency: call 911. Our page on [hangover shakes](/never-hungover/hangover-shakes) explains how to tell ordinary next-day tremor from withdrawal tremor.

## Who Is More Likely to Get Panic Attacks After Drinking?

Anyone can have one, but some people are more prone:

- **People with an anxiety disorder or panic disorder.** If you already have panic attacks, a hangover is a powerful trigger.
- **People who drink to manage anxiety.** Using alcohol to calm social nerves can backfire, because the rebound the next day is often worse than the anxiety you started with. Our guide to [alcohol and anxiety](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-anxiety-breaking-the-cycle-naturally-2025) covers this cycle.
- **People who drank a lot, fast, or on an empty stomach.** Bigger, faster blood alcohol swings mean a bigger rebound.
- **People who slept badly.** Short or broken sleep makes the nervous system much jumpier.
- **People who mixed alcohol with other substances**, especially stimulants, cannabis, or lots of caffeine.
- **People taking certain medicines.** Some antidepressants and other medicines interact with alcohol in ways that can increase side effects. If you take any regular medication, ask your doctor or pharmacist how alcohol fits with it.

## How to Prevent a Panic Attack After Drinking

No method guarantees you won't have one, but these steps tackle the specific causes above.

### Before and during drinking

- **Eat a proper meal first.** Food slows how quickly alcohol enters your blood and helps keep your blood sugar steadier overnight.
- **Pace yourself.** Roughly one standard drink an hour, with water in between, keeps your blood alcohol from spiking and crashing.
- **Set a limit before you start.** Panic after drinking tends to follow heavier nights. Fewer drinks is the single most reliable fix.
- **Avoid energy drink cocktails and stimulants.** They add caffeine and adrenaline on top of alcohol.
- **Don't drink to calm social anxiety.** It works for an hour and costs you the next day.

### Before bed

- **Drink a glass or two of water.** Keep some by the bed.
- **Have a small snack** if you didn't eat much.
- **Give yourself time.** Stopping drinking an hour or two before bed helps your sleep.

### The next morning

- **Eat breakfast**, even if it's small.
- **Go easy on coffee.** Have half your usual amount, or wait until you've eaten.
- **Plan a quiet morning** if you know you're prone to panic. Avoid diving straight into stressful emails or messages.
- **Get some daylight and a gentle walk.**

For more on the evidence behind these habits, see our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## When Panic Attacks Keep Coming Back

One panic attack during a rough hangover is unpleasant but doesn't, on its own, mean anything is wrong with you. It's worth talking to a doctor if:

- You get panic attacks **most times** you drink.
- You've had attacks **when you haven't been drinking**.
- You spend a lot of time **worrying about the next attack**.
- You've started **avoiding** places, people, or situations because of panic.
- You find yourself **drinking to cope** with the anxiety.

Panic disorder is common and very treatable. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), a talking therapy that teaches you to change how you respond to panic sensations, has strong evidence behind it. Some people also benefit from medicine. A doctor can check for physical causes such as thyroid problems or heart rhythm issues, and help you work out what fits you.

It also helps to look honestly at the pattern. If panic reliably follows drinking, the simplest experiment is to cut back for a few weeks and see whether the attacks fade. Many people find that drinking less, or more slowly, makes a bigger difference than anything else they try.

## Where Supplements Fit (An Honest Take)

Supplements aren't a treatment for panic attacks, and you should be skeptical of any product that claims to fix them. Here's what's known about the options people ask about most:

- **Magnesium** is involved in nerve and muscle function, and heavy drinking can lower it. Some people find magnesium glycinate in the evening helps them feel calmer, though evidence for hangover anxiety specifically is limited. See our [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol) guide.
- **L-theanine**, found in tea, is popular for mild stress. Research in people is small and mostly not about hangovers.
- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. A 2012 study in rats, published in the *Journal of Neuroscience*, found it counteracted some of alcohol's effects on the brain's GABA receptors, the same system involved in the rebound described above. That's why some people take it before drinking in the hope of a calmer next day. But there is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats panic attacks in people, and human research overall is limited. It doesn't replace drinking less, eating, sleeping, or seeing a doctor. If you want to try it as part of a sensible drinking routine, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much people take and when.

If you take any prescription medicine, especially for anxiety, depression, or sleep, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding a supplement.

## The Bottom Line

A panic attack after drinking is usually the result of several things landing at once: your brain rebounding from alcohol's calming effect, stress hormones, a heart that's already racing, poor sleep, low blood sugar, and often too much coffee. It feels terrifying, but it peaks within minutes and passes. Slow breathing, grounding, water, food, and rest help most. Don't drink more to calm down, and don't mix alcohol with anxiety medicine.

Take the warning signs seriously. Chest pain, fainting, an irregular heartbeat, confusion, or symptoms that won't settle need emergency care. Panic and shakes that come back every time you stop drinking can be withdrawal, which needs a doctor. And if panic attacks keep showing up after drinking, the most effective fix is usually the simplest: drink less, drink slower, and talk to a doctor if it keeps happening.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why do I get panic attacks after drinking?**

Alcohol calms the brain at first by boosting its main calming signal (GABA) and damping its main excitatory one (glutamate). As the alcohol wears off, the brain swings the other way and becomes temporarily over-excited. Add stress hormones, poor sleep, low blood sugar, dehydration, and a heart that is already beating faster, and the body can produce the full set of panic sensations. Many people then read those sensations as danger, which releases more adrenaline and tips it into a panic attack.

**Is a hangover panic attack the same as hangxiety?**

Not quite. Hangxiety is a low, lingering worry the day after drinking: replaying the night, dread, restlessness. A panic attack is a sudden surge of intense fear that peaks within minutes and comes with strong physical symptoms such as a pounding heart, shortness of breath, shaking, dizziness, or a feeling of doom. They share causes, and hangxiety can build into a panic attack, but a panic attack is sharper, shorter, and more physical.

**How long does a panic attack after drinking last?**

A single panic attack usually peaks within about ten minutes and eases over the following half hour or so, although you may feel shaky and drained for a while afterward. The background jumpiness of a hangover can last most of the next day. If intense symptoms keep going for hours without easing, or you have chest pain, fainting, or confusion, get medical help rather than assume it is panic.

**How can I tell if it's a panic attack or a heart problem?**

You often can't be sure on your own, and that's fine. Panic attacks tend to rise and fall within minutes and often ease with slow breathing. A heart problem is more likely if there is crushing chest pain or pressure, pain spreading to the arm, jaw, or back, fainting, an irregular pulse, or symptoms that don't settle. Alcohol can trigger a heart rhythm problem called atrial fibrillation. If you're unsure, especially the first time, call 911 or get checked. Doctors would much rather rule out a heart problem than have you wait.

**Should I drink again to stop a panic attack?**

No. A drink may blunt the feeling for an hour or two, but it delays the rebound rather than fixing it, and it trains your brain to link relief with alcohol. If you drink heavily most days and need a drink to stop shaking, sweating, or panic as alcohol wears off, that can be alcohol withdrawal, which can be dangerous. Talk to a doctor rather than managing it on your own.

**Can I take Xanax or other anxiety medicine for a panic attack after drinking?**

Not while there's still alcohol in your system, and not without a prescriber's guidance. Benzodiazepines such as Xanax (alprazolam) and alcohol both slow breathing and the brain, and the combination can be dangerous. If you have a prescription and get panic attacks after drinking, ask the doctor who prescribed it how and when it is safe to use.

**Does DHM help with panic attacks after drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents or treats panic attacks. DHM has been studied in rats for its effects on the brain's GABA receptors during alcohol exposure, which is why some people are interested in it for next-day anxiety, but human data is limited. If you have panic attacks, the strategies with real evidence are drinking less, sleeping, eating, slow breathing, and, if they keep happening, talking to a doctor about panic disorder.

**Do panic attacks after drinking mean I have panic disorder?**

Not necessarily. One panic attack during a bad hangover doesn't mean you have panic disorder. Panic disorder involves repeated, unexpected attacks plus at least a month of worrying about the next one or changing your life to avoid them. If attacks are happening when you haven't been drinking, or you've started avoiding places or situations because of them, that's worth discussing with a doctor. Panic disorder is common and treatable.
